articles.title: Sony completes acquisition of Crunchyroll from AT&T
articles.summary: Following the news that Sony was set to buy AT&T’s anime streaming service Crunchyroll, the completed acquisition brings together two powerhouse anime streaming services. Sony’s deal to acquire Crunchyroll was first announced in December 2020 and is valued at $1.175 billion.
articles.body: Sony officially owns AT&T’s Crunchyroll. Sony’s deal to acquire Crunchyroll was first announced in December 2020 and sees Crunchyroll join Funimation, Sony’s existing anime streaming property, under one roof. The ultimate goal of the unification of the two anime properties under a single roof is to develop “a unified anime subscription experience as soon as possible,” said Tony Vinciquerra, Chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment, in a statement. The deal is priced at $1.175 billion, and AT&T — which had been reported by The Information to be shopping the service around for $1.5 billion — will use the funds to help pay down the debt it amassed from its spending on streaming. In a radical shift away from its streaming strategy, AT&T has since decided to release its media assets and focus on its core connectivity business. Meanwhile, Sony plans to use the Crunchyroll service to broaden its already substantial anime streaming footprint. “With the addition of Crunchyroll, we have an unprecedented opportunity to serve anime fans like never before and deliver the anime experience across any platform they choose, from theatrical, events, home entertainment, games, streaming, linear TV — everywhere and every way fans want to experience their anime,” Vinciquerra said.

articles.title: Not even Spotify is safe from AI slop
articles.summary: Artists such as Standards, Health, Annie, and Swans have had AI-generated albums that aren’t theirs showing up on their Spotify pages. Why?
articles.body: I first noticed something weird when a HEALTH album dropped on my Spotify new release radar. Except the cover design was funny — it didn’t look like a HEALTH album. And it wasn’t. [Image: A screenshot of the fake Annie album, taken October 12th. Some kind of AI slop had been uploaded to HEALTH’s artist page on Spotify, one of three fake albums that would appear under their name that weekend. The band’s X account made some jokes about it, the albums were eventually removed, and I went back to minding my own business. Then, the next weekend, I saw a new Annie album had dropped. That album was more plausible — Annie had just released a new single, “The Sky Is Blue” — but when I clicked in, I couldn’t find it on the list of the song titles. Confused, I played the album and heard birdsong and a vaguely New Age-y instrumental. That… did not sound like Annie. So I did what any normal person would do: I bitched about it in my group chat. Which was how I heard that this was happening to other artists, like a lot of artists, and had been happening for months. (“I get one of these in my release radar often,” my buddy Gordon said.) For a while, metalcore artists such as Caliban, Northlane, and Silent Planet had been targeted. But so had a lot of artists with single-word names, such as Swans, Asia, Standards, and Gong. A new album would appear on an artist’s Spotify page, bearing their name but no similarity to their music. Sometimes, as with the fake HEALTH albums, they would disappear after a few days. Other times, they would linger indefinitely, even against the artist’s will. [Image: Can you spot the fake? “It was super weird,” says Marcos Mena, Standards’ lead songwriter and guitarist. “I thought, ‘Oh, this is something Spotify will take care of.’” After all, Standards has a verified artist page. But when a fake album was posted on September 26th, it didn’t budge. Mena emailed Spotify to tell them there’d been a mistake. The streamer responded two weeks later, on October 8th: “It looks like the content is mapped correctly to the artist’s page. If you require further assistance, please contact your music provider. Please do not reply to this message.” As of November 8th, the fake Standards album was still right there under the band’s verified, blue-checked name. It was finally removed by November 11th. “That was upsetting to me, because if you have ears, you can definitely hear it’s not our music,” Mena told me. “It’s definitely a bummer because we did have a new album come out this year, and I feel like it’s detracting from that.” What if someone came to a concert where Standards was opening for another band, went to Spotify to check out more tunes, and got the fake album instead? [Image: Can you spot the fake? To me, this all raised an obvious question: fucking why? Given the history of scams on Spotify, I think the answer is money. (The answer is almost always money.) To understand how this works, you need a sense of the mechanics. Streaming platforms like Spotify don’t work like your Facebook page — Mena and other artists aren’t logging in and adding albums to their accounts directly. Instead, they go through a distributor that handles licensing, metadata, and royalty payments. Distributors send songs and metadata in bulk to the streaming services. The metadata part is important; it includes things such as the song title and artist name but also other information, such as the songwriter, record label, and so on. This is crucial for artists (and others) to get paid. But this whole process effectively works on the honor system, and for something like the fake Standards album, this is where the problems begin. A distributor takes you at your word that you are who you say you are, Spotify takes the distributor at their word, and boom, there’s a fake album on a real artist’s page. Most of the time when this happens, it’s an honest mistake. In the recent spate of fakes, though, it seems like artists are directly targeted. Because the money an artist receives for streams goes through the distributor, the fake Standards album — should it get any payout at all — will reward someone other than Mena. We know the real Standards are on Topshelf Records, but the fake appears to be on something called Gupta Music, so Standards’ real label isn’t getting a cut, either. If enough people stream the album, the royalties will flow straight to Gupta Music… along with the payout from hundreds of other releases full of slop. Mena said he’d filed with his distributor to have the fake Standards album taken down. But whoever did it — Spotify or his distributor — didn’t notify Mena; I did, when I asked if he’d been involved in the removal. He wasn’t, he texted me, “but yayyyyy someone did something.” Going to Every Noise at Once — essentially an encyclopedia of what’s on Spotify — and searching for Gupta Music, I saw more than 700 releases. The cover art looked remarkably similar and smacked of AI. The purported band names were mostly one word: “Rany,” “Living,” “Bedroom,” and “Culture.” The albums shared names with the faux bands. A search for “Gupta Music” returned only a 14-year-old TED Talk by a man named Robert Gupta. [Image: Screenshot of Every Noise at Once, before the albums were removed. Even the supposed label name struck me as suspicious. There’s a well-known marketing agency called Gupta Media. It reps entertainment companies including Disney Music Group, Republic Records (in service of The Weeknd’s album), and Sony Music. In an email to The Verge, Gupta Media spokesperson Carly Carioli confirmed the agency “has no connection” to Gupta Music. “To be clear, Gupta Media is not now nor have we ever been involved in any of the activity you’re addressing — i.e., uploading fake music by fake artists to the profiles of real artists,” said Carioli. It looks like Standards, Annie, HEALTH, Swans, and a number of other notable one-word artists were targeted directly. Spotify confirmed that the onslaught of AI garbage was delivered from one source, the licensor Ameritz Music. Ameritz Music did not respond to a request for comment. “Due to significant and repeated violations of Spotify’s Metadata Style Guide, we ended our relationship with the licensor that provided the content in question,” said Chris Macowski, Spotify’s global head of music communication, in an emailed statement. “As a result, the content was removed from our platform.” Macowski also said that Spotify “invests heavily in automated and manual reviews” to prevent royalty fraud. Earlier attempts focused on metalcore musicians such as Fit for an Autopsy, Alpha Wolf, and Like Moths to Flames also seem like a coordinated attempt to siphon off legitimate streams. The culprit in that case was Vibratech Musicians, according to Idioteq. Each individual payout for a song stream on Spotify is tiny, as legitimate musicians who use the platform frequently lament. But hundreds or thousands of songs with relatively modest streaming numbers, when combined, can lead to big payouts. A fraudster just has to upload music and find a way to make accounts play it. And this doesn’t just happen on Spotify. There are more than 100 streaming platforms where artists can run this scam. In early November, Universal Music Group (UMG) sued Believe, a music distributor, and its US subsidiary TuneCore. In that lawsuit, UMG alleges Believe has a “conscious business strategy of indiscriminately distributing and purporting to license tracks with full knowledge that many of the clients of its distribution services are fraudsters.” The suit is about copyright infringement, and the details in it are striking. UMG alleges that artists such as “Kendrik Laamar,” “Arriana Gramde,” “Jutin Biber,” and “Llady Gaga” are among those Believe uploaded — suggesting a strategy of attempting to capture streams from users who had simply typoed. Another strategy is creating AI covers of popular songs and getting them onto popular playlists so normal people will stream them. Another involves bots “listening” to songs. Earlier this year, a Danish man was sentenced to 18 months in prison for using bots to get about $300,000 in royalties. Another man, Michael Smith, was arrested and charged with defrauding streaming services out of $10 million over the course of seven years. Smith used AI tools to create hundreds of thousands of songs under the names of fake artists such as “Calm Baseball,” “Calm Connected,” and “Calm Knuckles.” He then streamed the huge catalog using bots, billions of times, prosecutors allege. That diverted money that should have gone to real musicians that real people were really listening to. (In this case, Spotify paid only $60,000 to Smith, suggesting the company’s protective measures worked to limit payments, Macowski said.) “People upload massive amounts of albums that are intended to be streaming fraud albums,” says Andrew Batey, the CEO of Beatdapp, a company that aims to prevent streaming fraud. Batey estimates that $2 billion to $3 billion is stolen from artists through this kind of fraud every year. Distribution plays a big role. Most distributors’ business models are based on getting a cut of whatever royalties come back to the artists and labels. “Even though they may not be participating in the fraud, they directly benefit from it,” Batey says. In its suit, UMG alleges that Believe “wrongfully collects royalties it knows are properly payable by digital music services” such as UMG on copyrighted material. A sophisticated fraud operation will use multiple fake labels and multiple distributors in order to avoid having a single point of failure. Besides bot accounts, a number of bad actors have access to real people’s compromised accounts. “They log in as you and me, play their song three times and leave,” Batey says. That fake stream is then hidden among all the real listening the real account is doing. Gupta Music wasn’t the only label I found doing bulk uploading. There were three more doing something similar: Future Jazz Records, Ancient Lake Records, and Beat Street Music. All had also uploaded hundreds of albums with AI-looking album art. It’s unclear how these labels intended to generate streams, if at all. By the time of publication, most of those albums had been removed. Problems with metadata have existed for years — some of them innocent, some considerably less so. “We’ve basically gotten lucky so far,” says Glenn McDonald, a former Spotify employee who runs Every Noise at Once. “The content validation system without any input on the artist level is fairly crazy.” When something goes wrong, there are two levels where it can be addressed: the streaming service and the distributor. Distributors have to strike a delicate balance. They make their money by getting a cut of the streaming payout. If they are too aggressive in policing the uploads, legitimate artists get caught. Fixing that is expensive, and distribution is a low-margin, bulk business, McDonald says. But allowing too many junk bands through creates problems with the streaming services. As for the streaming services, they usually have data that could allow them to sort this out. If, for instance, the distributor that usually uploads Standards albums isn’t the one used for the new album, that’s the kind of thing that could be used to flag the album for review. (So is the change in label.) McDonald told me he also built tools for Spotify to identify when a song doesn’t sound like the rest of an artist’s catalog. Sometimes that can happen for legitimate reasons; an EDM remix of an Ed Sheeran song isn’t going to sound like Ed Sheeran, but it may still have happened with the label’s and artist’s approval. Also, some legitimate artists share the same name, especially tiny indie bands, and they just have separate pages. “The way it should have worked, getting the plumbing right, is that all those albums should have been flagged as new artists, and then it wouldn’t matter,” McDonald told me. As for the distributors, the thing to keep an eye on is UMG’s lawsuit. A pretrial conference is scheduled for January. The outcome of the suit could potentially change how distributors filter the music people try to upload through their platforms — because if lawsuits are more expensive than content moderation, there’s likely to be more content moderation. That could improve things for Spotify, which is downstream of them. Just banning AI-generated content from Spotify — or distributors — might feel like an intuitive solution. But despite the backlash against AI-generated media, there are legitimate AI-generated songs. For instance, “10 Drunk Cigarettes,” from Girly Girl Productions, is something of a hit. (It also is likely human-assisted, rather than wholly AI-generated.) UMG has made a deal with Soundlabs to allow artists to use Soundlabs’ AI vocals for themselves. It’s also partnered with Klay Vision to create a model for generating music. Besides, AI is just an accelerant for a type of fraud that’s lived on Spotify for years, says Batey. Fraudsters used to dig up old, obscure albums and digitize them or slightly alter a song that already existed. AI has just cut down on the amount of work that’s required to make the fake song needed to get the streaming money. At the same time… accelerants sure do make things burn down faster. Plenty of platforms have become less useful as they’ve been choked with AI glurge — Facebook, Instagram, the artist formerly known as Twitter, even Google itself. AI music poses the same threat to Spotify, McDonald says. He points out that I had been waiting for the Annie album, excited for it, even. And then instead, I got duped into garbage. “There’s all these mechanisms around assuming this stuff is correct,” he says. But right now, those mechanisms are broken — and people who truly care, like artists themselves, don’t have their hands on the controls. Update November 15th: Adds emailed statement from Gupta Media. Correction November 15th: The original version of this story referred to Carly Carioli as a spokeswoman. Carioli uses he/him pronouns.

articles.title: Musical sobre Gonzaguinha tem vigor cênico, a ideologia firme do artista e a marca da Barca dos Corações Partidos | G1
articles.body:
Cena do musical 'Gonzaguinha É', em cartaz na cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ) pela Cia. Barca dos Corações Partidos — Foto: Marcelo Rodolfo / Divulgação

Dramaturgia: Braulio Tavares e Ana Carbatti

Direção musical: Alfredo Del-Penho e Beto Lemos

♬ É tamanha a grandeza do cancioneiro do compositor Luiz Gonzaga do Nascimento Júnior (22 de setembro de 1945 – 29 de abril de 1991), o Gonzaguinha, que tem-se a sensação de que a Cia. de teatro Barca dos Corações Partidos tentou encaixar o maior número possível de músicas no roteiro de “Gonzaguinha É”, ainda que algumas composições sejam ouvidas quase como citações no espetáculo em cartaz de quinta-feira a domingo no Teatro Sesc Ginástico, na cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ).

Musical que abre hoje, quarta-feira, 7 de outubro, a 18ª edição da Festa Internacional de Teatro de Angra (Fita), “Gonzaguinha É” se desvia do formato tradicional do musical biográfico. Há, sim, informações sobre a vida e obra do cantor e compositor carioca, geralmente fornecidas ao espectador através de falas do próprio Gonzaguinha reproduzidas no texto assinado por Braulio Tavares com Ana Carbatti, dramaturga também no posto de diretora assistente.

Contudo, sob a direção inventiva de Inez Viana, o musical expõe a ideologia de Gonzaguinha em vez de refazer o percurso do artista de forma cronológica e convencional. E isso faz toda a diferença a favor do espetáculo porque o gênero vem dando sinais de repetição, necessitando ser oxigenado.

Com elenco que junta quatro atores pertencentes ao elenco da Barca dos Corações Partidos (Adrén Alves, Alfredo Del-Penho, Beto Lemos e Ricca Barros) com quatro atrizes convidadas para o espetáculo (Ana MaGa, Luiza Loroza, Nívea Magno e Thati Dias), o muslcal “Gonzaguinha É” é sustentado pela força do coletivo.

O canto conjunto de músicas como o samba “O que é o que é” (1982) – usado para arrematar a cena de forma contagiante, unindo vozes do palco e da plateia – e o bolero “Começaria tudo outra vez” (1976) se impõem sobre a maioria dos solos. Mas que ninguém espere números moldados para facilitar o coro da plateia. A Barca faz teatro, não karaokê.

De toda forma, há – em maior ou menor grau – brilhos individuais no canto do samba-enredo “O homem falou” (1985) por Thati Dias, na lembrança de “Pequena memória para um tempo sem memória” (1980) – espécie de réquiem de Gonzaguinha para a legião dos esquecidos na luta contra a ditadura de 1964 – na voz de Ricca Barros e no dueto em que Ana MaGa e Luiza Loroza ressignificam “Espere por mim, morena” (1976), dando sentido homoafetivo à canção meio toada que batizou álbum lançado pelo cantor há 50 anos.

Cena de 'Gonzaguinha É', musical em cartaz de quinta-feira a domingo no Teatro Sesc Ginástico, no Rio de Janeiro (RJ) — Foto: Marcelo Rodolfo / Divulgação

Musicalmente, sob direção de Alfredo Del-Penho e Beto Lemos, o musical se permite a liberdade de mandar “Recado” (1978) na batida do funk, no canto de Luiza Loroza, mas transita basicamente entre a cadência do samba do Rio de Janeiro (RJ), cidade natal de Gonzaguinha, e a intensidade árida ou festiva da música do Nordeste, região também entranhada na obra do compositor, filho de Luiz Gonzaga (1912 – 1989), rei do baião. O roteiro musical, aliás, parte do sertão, com “Galope” (1974) composição ouvida na voz de Del-Penho.

Muito da força do espetáculo reside no D.N.A. da Barca dos Corações Partidos. O movimento de corpo dos atores é uma das marcas da companhia teatral carioca evidenciada no espetáculo idealizado e produzido por Andréa Alves. Outra é a ausência de uma banda. Os atores / cantores tocam os próprios instrumentos e, da interação do elenco com os instrumentos e com os colegas, o espetáculo extrai um vigor cênico que o redime do fato de por vezes soar longo, mesmo não sendo longo.

Sobre todas as coisas, o que impulsiona “Gonzaguinha É” acaba sendo a ideologia entranhada nas letras e no pensamento do compositor. Essa ideologia sustenta e legitima o musical.

Gonzaguinha jamais fugiu à luta, tendo enfrentado o sistema em sambas como “Comportamento geral” (1972) – abordado nas vozes de Adren Alves e Ricca Barros – e entrado pelas brechas no campo do adversário, como em outro antológico samba dos anos 1970, “Geraldinos e arquibaldos” (1975), cantado por Nívea Magno em número que expõe a expressividade do trabalho de corpo dos atores da Barca. A propósito, a direção de movimento de Denise Stutz valoriza o espetáculo. O corpo também fala em “Gonzaguinha É”.

O expressivo trabalho de corpo do elenco fica evidenciado no musical 'Gonzaguinha É', espetáculo da Cia. Barca dos Corações Partidos — Foto: Marcelo Rodolfo / Divulgação

As músicas também falam por si só. O melodrama conjugal da canção “Grito de alerta” (1979), ouvida em aplaudido solo de Adrén Alves, bate direto no coração do público, assim como “Explode coração” (1978), outro hit infalível confiado à voz de Adrén. A exaltação do povo brasileiro no samba “E vamos à luta” (1980), cantado por Luiza Loroza, contagia. O humanismo repisado pelo compositor em “Caminhos do coração” (1982), solo de Alfredo Del-Penho, ainda enternece. Já o samba “É” (1988), puxado por Ricca Barros, tem potencial para soar mais empolgante em cena.

Enfim, o conjunto da obra de Gonzaguinha atravessa o tempo com força pela beleza de boa parte das músicas e pelas ideias propagadas nas letras. Construída com doses precisas de afeto e luta, essa obra é a matéria-prima que dá forma ao atual espetáculo da Barca dos Corações Partidos.

Em tempos de incerteza, “Gonzaguinha É” se mostra um espetáculo necessário como esse grande compositor que saiu de cena há 35 anos para ficar na história da música popular do Brasil.

Feito por oito atores, o musical 'Gonzaguinha É' se nutre em cena da força do coletivo — Foto: Marcelo Rodolfo / Divulgação

articles.title: Fãs do BTS 'adotam' banda de rock do ES e esgotam ingressos para show | G1
articles.standfirst: Banda 'The Skeep' viralizou após elogiar mobilização das 'Armys', fãs do grupo pop sul-coreano, que fizeram mobilização e passaram a seguir os capixabas nas redes. "É gratificante, sinal de que são bons tempos chegando", disse guitarrista.
articles.summary: Banda 'The Skeep' viralizou após elogiar mobilização das 'Armys', fãs do grupo pop sul-coreano, que fizeram mobilização e passaram a seguir os capixabas nas redes.
articles.body:
O que uma banda de rock de Marataízes , cidade do Espírito Santo conhecida nacionalmente como "capital dos abacaxis", tem em comum com o grupo de pop coreano BTS? A resposta é um verdadeiro exército de fãs de k-pop que conseguiu esgotar os ingressos do primeiro show da banda The Skeep fora das terras capixabas.

Marcado para acontecer em 29 de outubro, na capital de São Paulo, o evento teve 400 ingressos vendidos em seis dias e já conta com uma fila de espera de mais de 200 pessoas. Tudo isso graças aos fãs do BTS, que são conhecidos como "Army", e que significa "exército" em inglês.

Essa amizade improvável começou em agosto, quando o guitarrista Jhonny publicou um vídeo comentando sobre o poder de mobilização das fãs do grupo coreano e a dificuldade de o BTS fazer um show no Rock in Rio, já que as Armys são conhecidas por superar históricos de vendas de ingressos.

Na mesma publicação, o músico aproveitou para apresentar a própria banda de rock alternativo, The Skeep. Gratas pelo respeito que ele teve com o grupo estrangeiro, as fãs dos 'Bangtan Boys' viralizaram o vídeo e fizeram os perfis de Jhonny e da banda ultrapassar os 30 mil "follows" cada em apenas dois dias.

No início de outubro, The Skeep já somava mais de 45 mil seguidores no Instagram. "Eu era um roqueiro aleatório do interior do Espírito Santo que tocava para 30 pessoas. De repente, tenho uma banda que tem mais seguidores do que muita gente da minha cidade", disse Jhonny no vídeo (assista acima) .

De acordo com o último Censo do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), divulgado em 2022, a cidade de Marataízes tinha 41.929 habitantes.

"As Armys decidiram adotar a banda e a minha vida mudou completamente. No mesmo dia, fomos entrevistados por uma rádio e os fãs derrubaram o site da emissora devido ao alto número de acessos", relembrou Jhonny, em vídeo divulgado nas redes sociais.

Além do 'boom' nas redes sociais, a banda ganhou novos ouvintes nas plataformas musicais. A última música da The Skeep, "Vendaval No Box do Banheiro", já ultrapassou os 100 mil streams.

Kayo, o baixista da The Skeep, prometeu pintar o cabelo de roxo, cor do BTS, quando a música alcançasse essa marca. A promessa foi cumprida e os outros membros da banda também prometeram aderir ao visual em breve.

The Skeep, banda de rock alternativo do ES, viralizou após ser 'adotada' por fãs do grupo de k-pop BTS — Foto: Davi Souza

Aos poucos surgiu também toda uma comunidade, com direito a páginas de fã-clube, grupos nas redes sociais e produtos como chaveiros, camisetas e adesivos da The Skeep. Os membros da banda de rock ganharam até photocards, cartões colecionáveis com fotos dos ídolos, conhecidos no meio do k-pop.

Com a repercussão, a The Skeep decidiu fazer um show em São Paulo, marcado para 29 de outubro, na mesma semana das apresentações do BTS. O grupo sul-coreano se apresenta em São Paulo, no estádio do MorumBIS, nos dias 28, 30 e 31 de outubro.

"Tem muita gente nas redes dizendo que queria ir, mas não deu tempo de comprar ingresso. Para a gente isso é muito gratificante, um sinal de que são bons tempos chegando", comemorou o guitarrista Jhonny Nemesyz.

A mobilização mudou até o gosto musical. O guitarrista contaouque a banda passou a consumir mais das músicas do BTS e "se apaixonou" pelo grupo. "Ficamos encantados por essa comunidade calorosa que existe em torno do BTS e que tivemos a sorte de cativar de alguma forma", disse.

Em entrevista ao g1 , a The Skeep divulgou exclusivamente que vai lançar uma versão autoral de um dos sucessos do BTS, 'Like Animals' , com direito a videoclipe e muito rock. A regravação oficial será publicada no canal da banda no YouTube, no dia 17 de outubro .

A banda já publicou um cover da mesma canção no Instagram em um vídeo que alcançou 148 mil visualizações e mais de 26 mil curtidas, além de mais de 4 mil comentários. Muitos deles contam com 'emojis' de corações roxos, os preferidos das Armys.

"Tudo mudou. Já estamos com uma agenda de shows que só cresce, apesar de ainda não termos divulgado as datas. Todos os dias recebemos centenas de mensagens carinhosas de pessoas que passaram a conhecer a banda", concluiu Jhonny, grato pela transformação.

A banda de rock alternativo The Skeep começou em 2020 em Marataízes, no Sul do Espírito Santo. O grupo é formado por Jhonny Nemesyz (guitarrista), Barbara Ouzar (vocalista), Kayo Mattos (baixista) e Gabriel Akamarim (baterista).

Além de "Vendaval No Box do Banheiro", a banda também já emplacou a música "A Carta" e conta com canções como "Outra Parte de Nós" e "O Cara Certo na Cidade Errada".

articles.title: Rodas de samba, musical, regravações... por que está todo mundo homenageando Djavan? | G1
articles.standfirst: Artista completa 50 anos de carreira, e fãs optaram por oferecer flores em vida ao cantor alagoano de 77 anos. Entenda as motivações e veja os principais projetos.
articles.summary: Artista completa 50 anos de carreira, e fãs optaram por oferecer flores em vida ao cantor alagoano de 77 anos. Entenda as motivações e veja os principais projetos.
articles.body:
Djavan estreia na cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ) na noite de ontem, sábado, 1º de agosto, o show da turnê 'Djavanear 50 anos – Só sucessos' — Foto: Divulgação / Produção Djavan

"Me dê as flores em vida, o carinho, a mão amiga..."

Foi com a citação de um dos versos da música "Quando eu me chamar saudade", de Nelson Cavaquinho, que Arifan Júnior explicou o motivo da criação de uma roda de samba dedicada a tocar músicas de Djavan .

Criada no início de 2026, a "Pagodjafãs" é uma das homenagens feitas nos últimos meses ao cantor de 77 anos – 50 deles dedicados à sua carreira musical.

Mas para além disso, muitos outros artistas decidiram homenageá-lo: são rodas de samba pelo Brasil, regravações em diversos gêneros musicais, shows especiais, biografias e até um musical.

Mesmo o ano sendo uma efeméride para Djavan, tantas homenagens assim tendem a acontecer em maior número quando são póstumas.

E por que, então, tanta gente decidiu entregar flores em vida para Djavan neste momento?

Para o colunista Mauro Ferreira, "as pessoas estão tendo consciência de que um ciclo está se fechando."

"Está tendo uma passagem de bastão. Os grandes ídolos da MPB estão com, no mínimo 50 anos de carreira, quando não estão em 60. Então alguns já estão fora de cena por questões de saúde, como Milton Nascimento, outros já faleceram, como Gal Costa. E outros, como João Bosco, com 80 anos, e Djavan, com 77, estão fazendo uma revisão da obra, por mais que eles continuem em atividade."

"Acho que isso acende um alerta. Tipo: 'ó, esse cara está aqui, ele construiu uma obra gigantesca, ele está vivo, então vamos homenageá-los em vida'. Esse gatilho vem destas revisões que eles mesmos fazem", conclui Mauro.

O g1 conversou com alguns destes homenageadores para entender como a arte do cantor alagoano inspirou tantos projetos nos últimos meses e saber qual é a representatividade de Dja na vida de cada um deles:

Capa do álbum ‘Canto Djavan’, de Bruna Black, Hodari, Jonathan Ferr, Jota.Pê, Luccas Carlos e Melly — Foto: Pedro Figueiredo

Ainda em 2025, o álbum "Canto Djavan" ganhou o mund o. Jovens estrelas da música nacional, como Jota.Pê, Bruna Black, Hodari, Jonathan Ferr, Luccas Carlos e Melly, interpretaram algumas faixas do artista, e conseguiram trazer assinatura própria para as versões.

Ao g1 , Jota.Pê afirmou que o motivo que o fez topar participar do projeto foi, exatamente, o próprio Djavan.

"Ele é minha maior referência, fazer qualquer coisa que referencie ele é uma honra, então ser convidado para regravar duas músicas dele, num disco repleto de grandes artistas da minha geração? Impossível de recusar."

Jota escolheu regravar as faixas "Açai" e "Seduzir". Para o cantor, o fato de homenagear artistas ainda em vida é algo que vem aconteceu nos últimos anos e o deixa muito feliz. "Poder valorizar nossas referências em vida é necessário, celebrá-los em vida", diz.

Anitta e Tiee também trouxeram Dja para seus projetos recentes. Ao colocar o set com "Te Devoro / Linha do Equador / Avião / Maçã" em seu álbum "Uma Década Ao Vivo", Tiee explicou que o artista é uma de suas "maiores referências quando o assunto é música feita com alma".

Já Anitta escolheu traduzir para o espanhol a música "Azul" para entregar um presente para seu público latino, já que todas as outras faixas de EQUILIBRIVM II são em português. A cantora disse que "Azul" é sua faixa favorita do artista e se conecta com a vulnerabilidade, um dos temas que integram o álbum.

Roda de Samba Pagodjafãs na edição realizada em São Paulo — Foto: Reprodução/Intagram/Pagodjafãs/Shouriço

Thiaguinho já afirmou algumas vezes que Djavan "é muito pagodeiro" e interpretou algumas de suas músicas, como "Um amor puro", no projeto Tardezinha.

Além dele, outros pagodeiros e sambistas têm homenageado o artista em diversas rodas de samba em São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Salvador.

Uma delas, a Pagodjafãs, nasceu de forma despretensiosa, em janeiro, na ideia de celebrar os 77 anos do cantor.

"O encontro foi num bar que fica ali numa encruzilhada perto da Praça da Cruz Vermelha, de fãs (nós) pra outros fãs (que quisessem chegar), pra celebrar o aniversário do Dja. Conclusão: foi o caos! Pois em pleno dia de semana, a rua foi fechada por uma multidão de gente que ama Djavan", relembra Arifan Júnior, músico e um dos criadores da roda de samba “Pagodjafãs”.

"Djavan é quase a nossa religião. É um estado de espírito. Um portal de luz, onde a gente caminha por uma estrada de música linda e emocionante. E nessa viagem de prazeres, acessamos também lugares imprevisíveis no campo da imaginação, da poesia, da construção harmônica e de várias possibilidades", cita Arifan, explicando o motivo da homenagem.

"E pegando um gancho no trecho do samba de Nelson Cavaquinho [que aparece na abertura desta reportagem], a gente super pensou nessas flores em vida e nesse carinho ao nosso Djavan quando pensamos o nosso pagode."

Para Arifan, Djavan merece todas as homenagens. E considera todas válidas, independentemente dos gêneros musicais nos quais sua arte é colocada.

"Desde que façam com respeito e responsabilidade. Pois são as homenagens que levam o nome do Dja ainda mais longe, faz a galera querer buscar e aprender o lado B de mestre, e promove que a obra do mestre chegue em corações ainda não habitados pelo mesmo."

Djavan – O Musical: Vidas pra Contar chega a Salvador, nos dias 31 de outubro e 1 de novembro — Foto: Janderson Pires

Desde junho de 2025, o ator Raphael Elias roda o Brasil interpretando Djavan no espetáculo "Djavan – O Musical: Vidas pra Contar". Idealizado por Gustavo Nunes, o espetáculo recebeu 8 indicações na 13ª edição do Prêmio Bibi Ferreira.

Ao g1 , Gustavo contou que já fez outros espetáculos em homenagens a outros artistas ou bandas, como Cássia Eller e Paralamas do Sucesso.

"E, agora, o Djavan, um grande expoente da nossa cultura. Tivemos a vontade de homenageá-lo ainda em vida e vimos o quanto isso é importante. É uma grande satisfação, tanto para a gente quanto para ele, ver esse musical, que perpassa praticamente toda a vida e a obra dele, em 50 anos de carreira", conta Gustavo.

Além de celebrar o reconhecimento do próprio homenageado com a obra, ele considera que os depoimentos do cantor foram um grande diferencial para a construção do projeto.

"Tivemos a sorte de, com ele vivo, poder contar com a contribuição dele e com suas histórias. Não dependemos apenas da pesquisa. É claro que ela foi feita, mas pudemos falar diretamente com ele e saber mais sobre sua trajetória, a partir da fonte principal de tudo."

Mas o início não foi assim tão fácil. "No primeiro momento, ele achou estranho e não comprou muito a ideia. Mas depois entendeu a homenagem e como seria feita, gostou e embarcou no projeto."

A direção musical do espetáculo ainda leva assinatura de João Viana, filho de Djavan. "Ter a chancela da família é fundamental."

Antes de "Djavan – O Musical: Vidas pra Contar", outro musical, o "Djavanear - Um tanto flor, um tanto mar", já homenageava o cantor, ainda em 2023. Nele, Karen Julia, Leila Maria, Mattilla, Paula Santoro e Tontom Périssé traziam uma interpretação feminina do repertório do cantor.

Amanda Mendonça canta Djavan em show em homenagem ao cantor — Foto: Divulgação

As cantoras Amanda Mendonça e Vanessa Moreno decidiram dedicar as atuais fases de suas carreiras ao cantor.

Amanda está em turnê com um show todo voltado para o cancioneiro de Djavan. A ideia inicial era fazer um grande tributo a um artista da MPB. Como conterrânea do artista, a cantora alagoana não hesitou em escolher o artista.

"Além de ser um exímio cantor, compositor e intérprete, ele, igual a mim, fez o movimento de migrar de sua cidade natal [Maceió] em busca do sonho de viver de arte. Sendo assim, tenho muita identificação pelas histórias que suas letras e melodias contam, são uma inspiração para mim", explica a cantora.

"Acredito que precisamos valorizar os artistas em vida. É um legado que precisa ser compartilhado com as novas gerações."

"Quando pensei em um tributo, pensei em alguém vivo, que pudesse de alguma forma ver ou sentir minha homenagem a ele, por isso Djavan também, por sua tamanha sensibilidade e amor pela arte, para além de suas grandes obras e contribuições inigualáveis para a música popular brasileira e mundial", completa Amanda.

A cantora só lamenta que Dja ainda não tenha assistido sua apresentação. "Ficaria muito feliz e honrada. E seria um sonho cantar ao lado dele a música ‘Alagoas’ que ele fez em homenagem a nossa terra."

Vanessa Moreno canta nove músicas de Djavan em álbum gravado em estúdio com produção musical de Fi Maróstica — Foto: Rapha Moraes – O Filme Produções / Divulgação

Já Vanessa fez um álbum de regravações do artista depois de preparar um show dedicado às obras de Dja. "Comecei essa pesquisa de querer cantar músicas dele com quase 100 músicas. Aí fomos reduzindo, até chegar nas músicas do show, e depois, nas 9 músicas que compõem esse disco", explica.

A cantora, que tem "Azul" como uma das primeiras músicas que aprendeu a tocar no violão ainda na adolescência, diz que, para ela, Djavan representa "criatividade e liberdade". "Esse lugar de liberdade criativa que a música dele proporciona é muito inspirador pra mim."

Vanessa ainda analisou o fato de muita gente fazer críticas sobre a forma de compor do artista, mas, ainda assim, ele conseguir chegar a um público tão diverso e se conectar com vários gêneros musicais.

"O rebuscamento dele está justamente na simplicidade com que ele se comunica. Em relação às letras, é muito interessante porque ele não traz a coisa pronta. Ele traz imagens pra que a gente forme o significado na cabeça da gente com as informações que a gente tem, e a partir da atmosfera que ele fornece. Isso é muito rico."

"São melodias muito bonitas. Harmonias muito diferentes. E a rítmica muito presente nas composições dele fazem com que ele tenha uma maneira muito singular de ser música nesse planeta."

articles.title: Filme de Rondônia é único da América Latina em festival na Suíça | G1
articles.standfirst: Curta-metragem “Sussurros na Água” é o único representante da América Latina na categoria Intimacy Competition (Competição de Intimidade). Filme também é o único brasileiro selecionado para o festival.
articles.summary: Filme de Rondônia, "Sussurros na Água" estreia na Suíça como o único representante da América Latina na mostra competitiva de intimidade do festival.
articles.body:
Filme de RO 'Sussurros na Água' — Foto: Reprodução/Lucas Costa

Um filme produzido em Ji-Paraná (RO), terá sua estreia mundial em um festival internacional de cinema na Suíça. O curta-metragem documental "Sussurros na Água" será exibido pela primeira vez ao público na noite de 9 de outubro, durante o 19º Lust*streifen Film Festival Basel, na cidade de Basel.

A produção rondoniense foi selecionada para a mostra competitiva "Intimacy Competition" (Competição de Intimidade) e é o único filme brasileiro no festival e o único representante da América Latina nessa categoria . Ao todo, a competição reúne produções de diferentes países, entre eles Colômbia, Índia, França, Espanha, Alemanha, Bélgica, Austrália, Coreia do Sul, Nova Zelândia, Reino Unido e Estados Unidos.

O festival será realizado entre os dias 8 e 11 de outubro e chega à 19ª edição com o tema "Bodies in Solidarity" (Corpos em Solidariedade). O evento tem como proposta ampliar a visibilidade de histórias LGBTQIA+ no cinema e promover discussões sobre gênero, sexualidade e corpo.

Além da exibição de filmes, a programação conta com oficinas, rodas de conversa e outras atividades. O festival também possui uma mostra competitiva de curtas-metragens, que reúne produções suíças e internacionais.

O curta-metragem "Sussurros na Água" conta a história de dois homens que vivem uma relação marcada pelo desejo, mas que têm dificuldades para construir uma intimidade além dos encontros sexuais.

Produzido em Ji-Paraná, o filme mostra momentos da relação entre os dois e aborda sentimentos como solidão, expectativa, frustração e a vontade de encontrar uma conexão mais profunda.

A água aparece como um dos principais elementos da história. Rios e chuvas, tão presentes na vida de quem cresce na Amazônia, são usados para representar tanto acolhimento quanto a maneira como os sentimentos podem mudar e se transformar.

A produção também aborda as dificuldades enfrentadas por pessoas LGBTQIA+ para viver livremente seus sentimentos e relações, especialmente em ambientes onde ainda existe preconceito ou falta de espaços de acolhimento.

Dirigido por Otavio de Sousa, o curta foi construído junto com Cristiam Velozo, que participa da história. A relação entre os dois também fez parte do processo de criação do filme.

A cerimônia de abertura do festival ocorre na noite de 8 de outubro. A premiação está marcada para 11 de outubro.

articles.title: Evento em Noronha tem dança, teatro e música com entrada gratuita | G1
articles.standfirst: Segunda edição do Festival Internacional Cena Noronha acontece de quinta (8) a domingo (11), na Praça São Miguel, em Fernando de Noronha.
articles.summary: Segunda edição do Festival Internacional Cena Noronha acontece de quinta (8) a domingo (11), na Praça São Miguel, em Fernando de Noronha.
articles.body:
A segunda edição do Festival Internacional Cena Noronha será realizada de quinta-feira (8) a domingo (11), na Praça São Miguel, em Fernando de Noronha . O evento terá apresentações de teatro, dança e música, com entrada gratuita.

Segundo os organizadores, 75% das atrações são artistas e grupos da ilha, com destaque para produções inéditas. A programação também terá a participação da Marcelos Move Dance Company, grupo de dança formado por integrantes do Brasil e da Suíça ( veja vídeo acima ).

A ação é promovida pela Administração da Ilha. A gerente de Cultura, Anildeney Araújo, afirmou que o festival promove o intercâmbio cultural e contribui para fortalecer a economia criativa de Noronha.

“O objetivo principal é promover o intercâmbio cultural, dando espaço para os artistas de Fernando de Noronha e proporcionar uma vivência e apreciação de trabalhos produzidos fora da ilha, tanto nacionais quanto internacionais”, disse a gerente.

Evento será realizado em Fernando de Noronha a partir de quinta-feira (8) — Foto: Ana Clara Marinho/TV Globo

Anildeney Araújo afirmou ainda que o festival é voltado principalmente para os moradores de Fernando de Noronha, mas os turistas também podem acompanhar os espetáculos.

A programação reúne clássicos do balé e da dança contemporânea, teatro armorial inspirado na obra de Ariano Suassuna e apresentações de rock, reggae, forró, salsa, coco e maracatu.

articles.summary: Apoorva Mukhija, popularly known as The Rebel Kid, has broken her silence on the viral video of her kissing Amin Jaz.
articles.body: Apoorva Mukhija, popularly known as The Rebel Kid, has broken her silence on the viral video of her kissing Amin Jaz. In her latest vlog, she shared that the footage was shot at a private party roughly a year ago, and the two were completely unaware that they were being filmed. She remembered getting the news midway through her journey from Turkey to New York, while waiting out a layover in London. As a flood of messages about the clip arrived, she became overwhelmed and burst into tears at Heathrow Airport.Apoorva Mukhija breaks her silence on viral videoNeither Apoorva nor Amin knew a camera was rolling at the party, she said. "One of my videos from a year ago has gotten leaked. So this video was like a private moment between me and another guy. And we did not know that we were being recorded. This was at a private party," she said. The discovery left her stunned. "Aur ye video bohot purani hai. 1 saal purani hai aur ab aayi hai baahar (And this video is very old. It's about a year old and has surfaced now)," she said. When she reached London's Heathrow Airport, her phone was already flooded with people asking whether she had seen the clip. "My entire WhatsApp is filled with messages saying, 'Did you see this?'", Apoorva recalled.Apoorva Mukhija's parents watched the clip tooThings got even harder for Apoorva when she learned that her parents had watched the clip too. "This is the first time my parents saw that video. They did not know I had a boyfriend. They had no clue," she said. Coming on top of her private video suddenly spreading online, the realisation left her deeply shaken. Recalling that moment, she said, "So I have lost my mind."Apoorva Mukhija recalls crying amid the crowds at HeathrowSitting amid the crowds at Heathrow Airport, Apoorva said she struggled to process what had just happened. "I remember I sat at the Heathrow airport, and there were, I think, a million people at that airport. Aur main bas neeche baithke roye jaa rahi hu, roye jaa rahi hu (And I just sat there and kept crying and crying)," she recalled.Apoorva Mukhija and the India's Got Latent controversyBack in February 2025, Ranveer Allahbadia's jokes about parents and s*x on Samay Raina's India's Got Latent sparked intense backlash. articles.title: Dani García, chef: "Para que las lentejas queden más cremosas, hacemos un puré con el chorizo y la zanahoria y lo añadimos al final"
articles.standfirst: Dani García tiene un sencillo truco para conseguir unas lentejas más cremosas y potenciar su sabor sin cambiar la receta tradicional
articles.summary: Dani García tiene un sencillo truco para conseguir unas lentejas más cremosas y potenciar su sabor sin cambiar la receta tradicional
articles.body: Con la llegada del otoño, los platos de cuchara vuelven poco a poco a las cocinas españolas. Entre ellos, las lentejas siguen siendo uno de los clásicos que aparecen con más frecuencia cuando bajan las temperaturas. Cada casa tiene su propia receta, pero Dani García tiene un truco para conseguir que el guiso quede más cremoso y que el sabor del chorizo se integre de una forma diferente. El chef malagueño mostró esta técnica en 'Hacer de comer', el programa que presentó en La 1 de TVE. Su propuesta parte de unas tradicionales lentejas a la riojana, pero introduce un paso poco habitual: retirar el chorizo y la zanahoria después de cocerlos con las lentejas y triturarlos juntos para preparar un puré. La clave está en que el chorizo no termina simplemente cortado en rodajas dentro del plato. Una vez cocido, se pela y se tritura junto con la zanahoria y un poco del caldo de las propias lentejas. El resultado es una mezcla cremosa que puede incorporarse al guiso o servirse junto a él. García explicó que le gusta que las lentejas tengan "algún punto cremoso" y que para conseguirlo utiliza precisamente el chorizo y la zanahoria cocidos para elaborar ese puré. La elaboración comienza cociendo las lentejas con el chorizo, las zanahorias y una hoja de laurel. Mientras tanto, el chef prepara el sofrito por separado con ajo, cebolla, puerro, pimiento rojo, tomate, pimentón dulce y pulpa de ñora. Esta separación permite que las verduras se cocinen y concentren sus sabores antes de mezclarlas con las legumbres. Una vez cocidas las lentejas, llega el momento fundamental de la receta. Se retiran el chorizo y las zanahorias de la cazuela. El chorizo se pela y se tritura junto con las zanahorias y un poco del caldo de cocción hasta conseguir una textura similar a la de un puré denso. La receta original de 'Hacer de comer' utiliza 300 gramos de lentejas, 250 gramos de chorizo, tres zanahorias, dos zanahorias baby, un tomate, una cebolla, un puerro, un pimiento rojo, dos dientes de ajo, una hoja de laurel, un litro de caldo de carne, 15 gramos de pulpa de ñora, una cucharada de pimentón dulce, aceite y sal. El procedimiento tampoco requiere una elaboración especialmente complicada. Las lentejas se cuecen durante aproximadamente 30 minutos y, mientras tanto, se prepara el sofrito. Después se retiran el chorizo y las zanahorias para preparar el puré y se terminan de integrar las lentejas con el sofrito.

articles.title: Nathan Fielder Needs the Audience to ‘Help Me Understand What I Went Through’ in Making Elizabeth Holmes Doc
articles.summary: "It was a really disorienting experience," Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim said at a buzzy "You Can See Everything" screening
articles.body:
A24 hosted an early screening of Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder's buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary " You Can See Everything " at the David Geffen Theater at the Academy Museum Tuesday night. The event comes exactly one month after the film — which hadn't even been announced to the public yet — debuted as a secret screening at Telluride Film Festival, instantly rocketing into the awards race.

Years after filming, Fielder still can't make heads or tails of it.

"I still am not sure to this day what I experienced," Fielder told the crowd at a Q&A. "Maybe it being out there, everyone can help me understand what I went through a little bit. What we all went through."

Fielder and Oppenheim sat in conversation with Bill Hader after the film, revealing their magic tricks to a nearly full crowd (a rare feat for a late-night Q&A). Numerous stars turned out for the screening, held just over a week before the film hits theaters, with Zach Cregger, Adam McKay, Patrick Ball, Hannah Einbinder and Aidy Bryant among those seen in attendance. Everyone wanted to see what Fielder and Oppenheim had in store so soon after the latter released "Primetime," his equally buzzy film starring Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen. The room was not left disappointed.

We won't disclose spoilery details for that film, but we did learn a bit more about how it even came to be. Oppenheim said that he reached out to Fielder after he saw that the "Nathan for You" creator watched his debut feature, "Some Kind of Heaven."

"I was like, man, we should make something together," Oppenheim said of reaching out to Fielder. "I threw some ideas at him, and he didn't like any."

But, as fate would have it, an idea soon came to them. Fielder invited Oppenheim to attend the Hollywood magicians' venue The Magic Castle, where one of the performers in a close-up magic room asked the audience for a suggestion of a name.

"Elizabeth Holmes!" one patron shouted out.

Oppenheim immediately recalled hearing, a day before, that the Theranos founder and her partner, Billy Evans, had just asked A24 if the studio wanted to make a documentary about Holmes' last days before going to prison.

"First off, why A24?" Oppenheim wondered. "Secondly, she hadn't been on camera in many, many years. I thought there could be something interesting about that."

"She hadn't talked to anyone," Fielder said. "She hadn't done any press or anything in I think seven or eight years at the time."

So Fielder and Oppenheim, in turn, went to A24, asking for a meeting with Holmes. Fielder still recalls the experience of meeting the one-time health tech mogul, who was sentenced to 11 years in prison for fraud, for the first time before cameras rolled.

"It was a really disorienting experience, talking to someone like that, when they seem so sincere," Fielder told the crowd.

There's a bit of irony in that. Fielder's claim to fame was initially "Nathan for You," a documentary series in which he approached struggling businesses with comedic "solutions" to help bring in more customers. He later followed this up with he HBO series "The Rehearsal," in which he constructed fabricated environments with the goal of helping people practice for life's stressful moments. Both of those shows involve an incredible amount of thought and manipulation from Fielder and his team, often yielding the question of where the show ends and the host begins. Oppenheim likewise played with the concept of the camera's clash with reality in "Primetime," a film interested in the ethics of Chris Hansen's televised predator-catching.

Oppenheim revealed that "You Can See Everything," much of which was filmed in 2023 before Holmes' imprisonment, didn't initially involve Fielder as much of an on-camera protagonist. Early on, however, cameras started wandering in Fielder's direction to help moor the audience amid the confounding characters of Holmes and Evans.

"The only way to make this work is to have someone confront their delusions," Oppenheim told the crowd.

When Fielder and Oppenheim went back to A24 about the project, they were shown an open door, told that they would be given resources to film Holmes and Evans, regardless of whether or not a film actually came out of it. This came together less than two months before Holmes' prison sentence began. Several times, Fielder said he offered to leave when things got heated or emotional, especially knowing that they had two young children at home. The duo repeatedly rejected Fielder's offer.

In fact, they invited Fielder to stay with them in their guest house for the duration of the filming (around 35 days in total). Oppenheim said that, at one point, they bought a $10 debugger to see if Fielder's room was wired to clue Evans into their crew's conversations. The cheap tool did not work, so they rolled the dice.

Fielder and Oppenheim expressed confusion at why Holmes wanted them there in the first place. They were also confused by just about everything they saw while there.

"The first place that we started from was like, 'Can we document this in a way that brings the audience into this experience?'" Oppenheim said. "That puts you in the house. That puts you into that feeling ."

The duo brought with them a crew of seven individuals to film the day-to-day of Holmes' life before incarceration, including cinematographer David Bolen, who shot Oppenheim's "Primetime." As Fielder, Oppenheim and their crew witnessed the same strange reality of Holmes and Evans' life, they hoped to collectively make some sense of what they were experiencing. But that sense never came.

"At the end of the day, Lance and I would talk about what had happened, and we would be on totally different sides of what we thought was actually happening and completely disagree on moments that we both witnessed," Fielder said. "That's when we were like, 'Oh, there's maybe something here in this if we just follow our natural curiosity with it all. That's interesting."

"It wasn't just us, that we couldn't agree on certain things," Oppenheim. "Even just really simple, mundane moments, everybody in our crew had different opinions about it."

"You Can See Everything" releases in theaters on Oct. 16.

articles.title: DJing is my first priority at this point of my career: Ali Mercchant
articles.summary: For Ali Mercchant, a performance in Hyderabad comes with a sense of familiarity.
articles.body: For Ali Mercchant, a performance in Hyderabad comes with a sense of familiarity. The actor-DJ was recently in the city for a show with Sunny Leone, where their respective performances came together on one stage. For Ali, though, Hyderabad is not simply another stop on his performance calendar. It is a city he has a longstanding connection with, both personally and musically. In a chat with us, he talks about the collaboration, his relationship with the city and the journey that has taken him from television and acting to finding his space behind the DJ console.‘Hyderabad is my second home’Ali’s recent Hyderabad performance with Sunny Leone brought together his DJ set with her performances of popular songs, accompanied by a group of dancers. “It was a great collaboration between Sunny and me. I had created a Sunny Leone mashup for the performance, and she performed to the songs along with the dancers,” he says.The show also brought him back to a city with personal significance. “Hyderabad is my second home. I met my wife (Andleeb Zaidi) here, so I will always have a soft corner for Hyderabad. I am always excited to perform here. Hyderabad has a lot of energy,” he says.‘Marfa gives that vibe of everybody celebrating together’That connection has also influenced his music, most notably leading him to experiment with Hyderabad’s marfa sound after his wife introduced him to it. “She said, ‘Why don’t you do something with this?’ and I thought, ‘Oh wow, this does sound really nice and exciting.’” After speaking to people in Hyderabad, he learnt that it was largely associated with weddings. “I wanted to shift that and make it more exciting for the younger generation as well as for everybody who had not experienced marfa.”When I see the mashups going to 10 million, 20 million, 30 million views and see that much love coming my way, I feel that whatever you do, as long as you are being appreciated, that is what satisfies an artiste- Ali MercchantHe combined the sound with Voices In My Head by Anyma, Argy and Son of Son with the mashup soon making waves in Hyderabad. “For me, music is always about togetherness. Marfa gives that vibe of everybody celebrating together. For Punjabis, it is ‘oh-ho-ho-ho’; in the same way, for Hyderabadis, I think it is marfa.”‘Just like an actor, I felt I could move people’s emotions as a DJ too’Ali’s shift to DJing followed years in television in shows like Kahaani Ghar Ghar Kii, Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai and more. “I used to do a lot of television. Obviously, I could see that television was dying, and I wanted to do things that were more creative and independent as a profession, as well as a performing talent.”What appealed to him about DJing was its ability to change an audience’s mood. “I loved the idea of how people, after the end of the day when they are really exhausted and tired, can have their mindset and tempo changed by a DJ. You can give them all the possible joys or move them along with their emotions. I felt that maybe I could do something similar as a DJ for a live audience. It clicked, it went well, and that is how my journey with it went in the most exciting manner.”‘I’m not saying no to acting’While acting remains on his radar, Ali says DJing is currently his top focus. “I think both are in the same phase, but right now, for the next phase of my career, I would actually say DJing is my first priority.” He also feels the nature of his audience’s response has changed. “I received the same amount of love when I used to do television. The only difference is that, at that time, it was for a particular character they loved and, obviously, for the particular channel they were watching. Now, the difference is that they are coming in for me.”Acting, meanwhile, remains open, provided the role interests him. He has completed a film produced by Nawazuddin Siddiqui’s brother that is currently on the festival circuit and hopes to return to reality shows. “If I get a very exciting role that really moves me, rather than something stereotypical that is happening currently, I would be interested,” he says, signing off.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Henar Álvarez lanza un dardo a Rufián en 'Al cielo con ella': "Cuando tienes a todo el mundo ilusionado, te haces el longuis"
articles.standfirst: La presentadora de RTVE cree que los políticos deben ser como unos “fontaneros” para la población
articles.summary: La presentadora de RTVE cree que los políticos deben ser como unos “fontaneros” para la población
articles.body: Henar Álvarez cree que los políticos de este país no cumplen muchos de los requisitos que exigen a la población. Por ejemplo, en plena crisis de vivienda, no pueden tener más de cinco pisos. “Conflicto de intereses se llama”, apunta en ‘Al cielo con ella’. Tampoco cree que lo más adecuado sea tener un seguro privado de médico o no haber obtenido sus títulos en un centro público. Y es que para la presentadora, los políticos en España deberían ser como los fontaneros. Es decir, “no puedes tener un fontanero en casa y después de un mes que te diga: ‘Jo, no lo puedo arreglar, es que no veas cómo te dejó el anterior el lavabo”. Y, en su opinión, esto está ocurriendo demasiado. Por encima del resto, Álvarez señala a uno de los políticos nacionales. “En lo de cumplir promesas también incluyo esto de dejar caer que te presentas y cuando tienes a todo el mundo ilusionado, hacerte el longuis”, asegura mientras mencionaba el nombre de Rufián entre una tos forzada. “Es que esto en mi barrio se llama ser un calientapoll*s, no sé en el vuestro”, zanja. A su juicio, el nivel de interlocuciones de los responsables políticos tampoco están dando el nivel: “Unas personas que se dedican a hacer discursos públicos, yo creo que tendría que estar prohibido decir gilipolleces. Por ejemplo, no puedes intentar hacernos creer que el cuchillo de untar el hummus es un arma homicida”. Una referencia clara a José Luis Martínez-Almeida. Tampoco se olvida de los representantes públicos que han visto en las redes sociales un nicho que aprovechar, como Óscar Puente. “Esto también incluye lo de andar haciendo el mamarracho en Twitter y TikTok. ¿Quieres gobernar o quieres un Premio Ídolo? Pues si quieres un Premio Ídolo, llamamos a Dulceida y acabamos antes”, bromea. De todo esto, Henar Álvarez saca una moraleja: “Dejad de llamar vagos a los de la acampada, que sois vosotros los que os tocáis la huevada”.

articles.summary: Michael Douglas reveals in his memoir "One Helluva Ride" that he called five women in one day to prove his commitment to Catherine Zeta-Jones.
articles.body: Michael Douglas didn’t just choose Catherine Zeta-Jones — he called five other women in one day to make sure she was the only one. The two-time Oscar winner pulls back the curtain on his extraordinary life in his new memoir, "One Helluva Ride," revealing his struggle to escape his father Kirk Douglas’ towering shadow, his past affairs and drug use, his terrifying battle with stage IV cancer — and the highs and lows of his decades-long love story with the actress. They welcomed their son, Dylan, that year, followed by their daughter, Carys, in 2003. Today, the couple split their time between New York, Mallorca and Santa Barbara. In the book, Douglas wrote that in 2013, the couple went on vacation and, upon returning, "had a heart-to-heart" about their relationship. "We had been married for more than a decade," Douglas recalled. "We had just gone through a period where a number of challenges came at us all at once. We decided to take some time apart. "Our marriage deserved a second chance. Today, our marriage is stronger than ever, and we recently celebrated our 25th wedding anniversary. We still love spending time together. articles.title: Google now lets you make games with AI
articles.summary: Google today announced Playground, a new browser-based platform for making custom games from AI prompts.
articles.body: Google today announced Playground, a new browser-based platform for making custom games from AI prompts. Playground will be available today in the US for users who are 18 and older at playground.google. The company is pitching it as an “experimental gaming platform” that “lowers the barriers to creation” and doesn’t require coding experience. “With Playground’s conversational interface, you can direct the game just by typing what you want to build,” Google says in a blog post. “Start from a blank canvas, remix starter prompts, or use guided support to shape your concept — and then test it right away. Want to tweak the physics, rewrite the rules, customize the characters, or overhaul the environment? Just ask. You stay in complete control of the creative direction from rough concept to final polish.” [Video: Google Playground demo showing a game being generated] When you’re finished making your game, you can share it with a link or publish it to the “Playground Explore gallery” so others can play it. “Select genres” will support in-game leaderboards and multiplayer. The gallery will highlight games that are “fresh, creative, and fun” using ratings and play activity, according to Google. Playground is free to use, but if you have a Google One subscription, you’ll have higher weekly token limits based on your plan, Google spokesperson Nia Carter tells The Verge. Under the hood, Playground is powered by “Google’s existing foundation models (Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria) paired with a custom harness refined through our own internally built games and evaluations,” Carter says. [Video: Google Playground demo video showing a game being played] Alongside today’s Playground announcement, Google and Unity are also revealing Unity Spark, an AI game-making experience that’s closer to a professional-level game development engine and allows you to create games simultaneously with others. Games made with Unity Spark will be shareable on Playground. A closed beta for Spark is scheduled to kick off later this year, and people who are interested can get on a waitlist starting today. Google’s news today follows Meta’s recent announcement that it will let users build games with AI on their phones and on the web for its Horizon platform with new apps rolling out in early access. Published games made with those tools will be able to be recommended on Facebook and Instagram, which could give them more reach than they would have just being on Horizon. Roblox has also started letting users make games with AI on their phones as part of a “Build” feature that’s in public alpha testing in a few countries.

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere's ex-fiance claims her jewelry was sold to pawn shop
articles.summary: Panettiere's ex-fiance filed a petition to be the guardian of their daughter.
articles.body:
Hayden Panettiere's ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko believes that someone outside of Panettiere's family sold some of her possessions, including her jewelry, to a pawn shop, according to a new court filing.

The claim is part of a new supplement to Klitschko's earlier petition with the Los Angeles County probate court, which was filed in September and sought to have him be made the temporary guardian of his and Panettiere's daughter, Kaya Klitschko, whom they welcomed in 2014. The petition had raised concerns about the preservation of the late actress' estate.

According to the new filing, the pawn shop has "declined to disclose specific item information without being contacted by law enforcement" and there's a risk that Panettiere's items "will be sold, transferred or otherwise rendered unrecoverable," causing a "direct financial detriment of Kaya."

In addition to seeking guardianship of his daughter, Klitschko is asking the court to grant him the ability to "request and authorize law enforcement investigation into the recovery of Hayden's property believed to have been misappropriated."

Panettiere died in August after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina apartment. The Greenville County Coroner's Office in Greenville, South Carolina, said in a statement the 36-year-old actress died as a result of an accidental overdose of drugs , including fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.

The investigation into Panettiere's death remains ongoing, with the focus likely shifting to the source of the fentanyl. Sources previously told ABC News the investigation could be honing in on street-level drug dealers who may have provided drugs to the late actress.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning is a tepid thriller that reminds us of how we got here
articles.summary: The Social Reckoning — in theaters October 9th — is a bleak reminder that we haven’t really reckoned with Facebook at all.
articles.body: When David Fincher’s The Social Network premiered in 2010, many people still thought of Mark Zuckerberg as a genius who had revolutionized the world by creating Facebook. Writer Aaron Sorkin’s script was critical of Zuckerberg’s character and his ruthless approach to doing business, but it also helped mythologize the co-founder at a time when the general public was much more enchanted by Silicon Valley. When Zuckerberg said in 2014 that he’d been hurt by the film’s depiction of him, Sorkin said he was “sorry that it did” and admitted that he “wouldn’t want a movie made about the things I did when I was 19 years old,” either. Sorkin”s apology was a reflection of how much grace the public was willing to extend to the world’s (then) youngest billionaire. But in 2026, it is hard to imagine anyone having all that much sympathy for the man running Meta. Similar to the way The Social Network spun details from Ben Mezrich’s book The Accidental Billionaires into a riveting drama, writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning weaves a narrative around The Wall Street Journal’s bombshell reporting with Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen. Billed as a companion piece rather than a direct sequel, The Social Reckoning chronicles Haugen’s time within Facebook and uses her story to illustrate how the company’s focus on exponential growth turned it into a societal threat. Zuckerberg looms large in the movie, but Sorkin feels far more interested in focusing on the friction that exists between traditional media and tech giants. Though The Social Reckoning’s core messages about how our lives have been negatively impacted by the rise of social media algorithms are potent, the film lacks the propulsive, thrilling energy that made The Social Network feel operatic. The film does an excellent job of presenting our present day reality as the end result of events Zuckerberg and Facebook helped facilitate. But for all of its insight, The Social Reckoning still feels like a feature that’s arriving a little too late to have a meaningful impact. [Media: The Social Reckoning spends much of its 112 minute runtime ping ponging back and forth through the years when Haugen (Mikey Madison) worked as a product manager on Facebook’s civic integrity team. As the film opens in 2019, Haugen’s just beginning to understand how hate speech and misinformation are being amplified by the platform’s algorithms. Haugen genuinely believes that Facebook could take steps to mitigate these harms if any of her colleagues would take them seriously. But when she realizes that no one else in the company is willing to speak up about Mark Zuckerberg’s (Jeremy Strong) single-minded focus on boosting Facebook’s engagement at all costs, she turns to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White). Sorkin presents Haugen and Horwitz as uneasy allies. The duo both understand that Facebook is the news for millions of people, but the only way they can report the truth about what’s happening within the company is by doing things the old fashioned way. You can hear echoes of Sorkin’s The Newsroom in Horwitz’s quippy exchanges with taciturn bureau chief Christina (Betty Gilpin) and overworked interns (Aidan Laprete, Kelley Pereira) about the importance of their work. The film frames its reporter characters as competent heroes who are trying to do the public an important service. It does not consistently do the same for the whistleblower, and Sorkin writes Haugen’s dialog with a degree of levity that often feels at odds with the gravity of the larger story. The Social Reckoning feels most like a proper thriller in tense moments when Haugen and Horwitz are secretly meeting in parks and hotel rooms to pore over damning internal documents detailing how Facebook was well aware of its products’ potential to do harm. The movie effectively depicts Facebook — in its pursuit for growth — knowingly becoming a place where conspiracy groups could thrive and radicalize people. Sorkin doesn’t go so far as to solely blame Facebook for turning the modern internet into a nightmare that’s flooded with ragebait and intentionally deceptive information. But The Social Reckoning does make the implicit argument that things might not be so bad today if Zuckerberg had acted more conscientiously in his quest to stay one step ahead of his competitors. [Image: Though Madison and White try their best to turn Sorkin’s script into dialog that sounds like it might be spoken by regular humans, the writer-director’s penchant for rapidfire back-and-forths gets the better of him here. Sorkin clearly wanted to make The Social Reckoning as dense with information as he possibly could, but in doing so, he made it harder for the movie to work as an entertaining drama. The Social Reckoning truly shines in its handful of scenes that zoom in on an older, more calculating Zuckerberg as he’s preparing to speak at Congressional hearings. Whereas Jesse Eisenberg played Zuckerberg in The Social Network with a quiet vulnerability, Strong leans into an unsettlingly robotic aura that makes his performance feel studied. Strong’s Zuckerberg gives you the distinct sense that he is a man whose success is a testament to his willingness to prioritize profit over people’s well-being. Especially for those who didn’t follow the Wall Street Journal’s Facebook reporting in real time, The Social Reckoning may serve as a useful recollection of how the company was — at one point, at least — held somewhat accountable for its actions. But the movie also serves as a bleak reminder of how there still hasn’t really been a substantive reckoning that fundamentally changed the way people interact with Meta’s (née Facebook) products. Sorkin seems to believe that a day may come when the public decides that companies like Meta can’t be trusted with the power to shape our perceptions of reality. It’s a hopeful thought, but in 2026, it feels like a dream that has already gotten away from us. The Social Reckoning also stars Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen, Patrick Fischler, and Nelson Franklin. The movie hits theaters on October 9th. Correction, October 7th: An earlier version of this article misstated that David Fincher apologized to Mark Zuckerberg. Aaron Sorkin is who apologized.

articles.title: Joe Manganiello Reveals 7-Year Battle with Mysterious Autoimmune Disease That He Says Nearly Killed Him (Exclusive)
articles.summary: “I can’t believe I’m alive,” Manganiello tells PEOPLE ahead of the release of his new memoir ‘Bloodlines,’ in which he chronicles his lengthy illness
articles.body:
Joe Manganiello is opening up to PEOPLE about his secret health battle that he says nearly killed him

The True Blood star says he's now symptom-free and engaged to Caitlin O'Connor after the 7-year-long ordeal

Manganiello's new memoir Bloodlines will be available everywhere on Oct. 13

Joe Manganiello 's long hair is tied up in a top knot, his beard is perfectly groomed, and his skin boasts glowing tan. He looks healthy because, finally, he is.

For seven of the last 10 years, the actor was secretly fighting a mysterious autoimmune illness so virulent it nearly killed him. In his new memoir Bloodlines (out Oct. 13), Manganiello, 49, opens up about recovering from a health battle that led to "major organ amputation" and contributed to the end of his seven-year marriage to actress Sofía Vergara , 54: "I can't believe I'm alive," he says. "I feel like I was reborn."

Manganiello first skyrocketed to fame in 2010 on True Blood as sexy werewolf Alcide Herveaux and then as a bare-chested stud in 2012's Magic Mike . In 2015, he married Modern Family star Vergara. Life was good—until Manganiello's health began to deteriorate shortly after their wedding.

It started with excruciating abdominal pain that left him unable to walk as his digestive tract ulcerated, along with fevers, blistering rashes, headaches and fatigue. He even began bleeding from his rectum while still a newlywed. "I was getting sicker and sicker," he says.

Over the course of seven years, Manganiello lost 60 lbs., underwent countless colonoscopies, and in one emergency surgery in 2016, had part of his intestines removed, leaving him unable to go to the bathroom normally and relying on an ostomy bag.

"It happened to me, and it's the truth, and I have all the scars to prove it," Manganiello says of the ordeal, for which he never received a conclusive diagnosis. "[Autoimmune] conditions are a dumping ground for things [doctors] don't understand. They start running you through this gauntlet of drugs."

Manganiello was prescribed meds for nerve pain as well as drugs used to treat Crohn's and colitis. "None of them worked on me," he says. Forced to turn to hydrocodone pills, fentanyl patches and marijuana to ease his agony, Manganiello wrestled with his hard-won 13 years of sobriety. "I didn't feel like I deserved to say that I was sober," he recalls, "[but] I had to put the pain and the condition first."

As Manganiello cycled through hospitals searching for answers, his illness took a toll on his marriage, which he writes had "become devoid of any emotionality whatsoever." He claims in the book that Vergara refused to hug him even when he begged and that she ridiculed him for his 5-lb. chihuahua Bubbles, a then-sickly pup Manganiello had adopted in 2019 when he was considering suicide. "I had to give my gun away because I kept thinking about it, and then the dog came. I went from being the patient to the caretaker," he says.

The couple's dream of having a child together had also been dashed. Vergara would later tell a Spanish newspaper that their marriage "broke up because my husband was younger; he wanted to have kids, and I didn't want to be an old mom." But Manganiello says he gave up the idea because of his illness. After failed IVF attempts led to them considering egg donors, he says he didn't want to die and leave Vergara with a child "who wasn't biologically hers."

Writing this book was his way of correcting the record: "There were things said and printed about me that were false," he says.

His marriage crumbling and his body failing, Manganiello looked beyond traditional medicine for answers. At one point his desperate search brought him to Cuba where a medicine man had him lick the pituitary gland in a goat's skull, but Manganiello believes he eventually found healing through a Santa Monica shaman, who told him generational trauma was to blame.

Manganiello's great-grandmother lost nine of her children to genocide in Armenia, and his grandmother battled lupus. He says he unburdened himself of his family's torment by confronting it: "Whatever chains there were to the past suffering of my ancestors, they were completely broken. There's not an ounce of fear in me about moving forward with my life."

Now the actor, who underwent follow-up surgery to reconnect his digestive tract, says he's off medication and symptom-free.

"Autoimmune diseases can go into remission," says Dr. Dawn Beaulieu, a Vanderbilt University Medical Center gastroenterologist and functional medicine provider who hasn't treated Manganiello. "From a medical standpoint, all we know is that he's better. This was his journey."

By his side on that journey today is Manganiello's fiancée Caitlin O'Connor , 37, whom he met after he filed for divorce in 2023. "Caitlin came into my life at this point where it was obvious to me that [she] was the direction to go," he says.

Together the couple are navigating a future—possibly one with children. "If that's meant for me," Manganiello says of potential fatherhood. "For seven years I thought I was going to be dead the next week. The world has opened back up to me."
